properties.decision:
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-07-31: an increment is cut when every item scheduled for it with `modality: required` is DELIVERED. Nothing else gates the cut, and no calendar does.

WHAT MAKES IT COMPUTABLE RATHER THAN A CONVENTION, and this is why it needs no new machinery: `SCHEDULED_FOR` already points at a `Release` as well as a `DesignEpoch` — the capability-increment axis beside the time axis, deliberately one edge type for both paired views — and `arrival_delta` already accepts either as its target. So the trigger IS `arrival_delta(release).missed_obligations == []`. `missed_obligations` is exactly the set of `required` claims that did not land, and `required` was already defined as an obligation whose miss is a computed violation rather than a slip (`dec:schedule-is-an-edge-with-modality`). The trigger is therefore read off the same computation that reports the delta, not asserted beside it.

EXPECTED items do NOT gate the cut. That is the whole point of the modality split: `expected` is a plan and may slip without stopping a release, `required` is an obligation and cannot. An increment with three expected items outstanding and no required ones is READY, and the outstanding three are reported rather than silently dropped.

`outstanding` ITEMS ARE A QUESTION, NOT A BLOCKER. An item still pointed at the increment, undelivered, that nobody has moved or dropped is neither deferred nor discontinued, and at cut time it is the question `req:plans-move-honestly` says must be ASKED and never defaulted: does it slip to the next increment, or is it withdrawn? If it was `required`, the cut does not fire until that is answered — because answering it either delivers the item or moves it, and both change `missed_obligations`.

REJECTED — A FIXED CADENCE (weekly, fortnightly). It cuts whether or not anything landed, and fails to cut when something did. `req:frictionless-update` asks for releases that are "frequent and very minor, so updating is routine rather than an event", and a calendar delivers neither half: it produces empty releases in quiet weeks and holds finished work back in busy ones. FREQUENCY IS A PROPERTY OF HOW SMALL THE INCREMENTS ARE SCOPED, not of how often the trigger is checked — which puts the frequency dial where someone can actually turn it.

REJECTED — ANY CONSUMER-VISIBLE CAPABILITY LANDING. Closest to `req:frictionless-update` in spirit and rejected on a specific inability: it cannot say "these three things ship together". A release whose trigger is "anything shipped" cannot express an increment that is only coherent when complete, and this project has already shipped such a pair — planned epochs are meaningless without the schedule that populates them.

WHAT THE TRIGGER DOES NOT DECIDE, deliberately: whether the increment is CORRECT. `req:released-eq-designed` (priority critical) and the CI gates are the quality bar; this is only the readiness signal. A green trigger on a red build is not a release, and nothing here overrides that.
properties.name: A cut fires when every REQUIRED item scheduled for the increment is delivered — the trigger is computed, not scheduled
properties.rationale:
Chosen from three put to Anthony, and the deciding argument is that this option is the only one already computable from what the design holds.

The other two would each have needed a new mechanism — a schedule to run the cadence against, or a rule for what counts as consumer-visible — and both would have sat beside the graph asserting something the graph could not check. This one is read off `arrival_delta`, which shipped the same day, and it gives `modality: required` its second job: it already made a miss a computed violation, and now it also decides when a release is ready. A vocabulary distinction that two computations read is exactly what `dec:edge-orthogonality` says earns its keep.

The cadence rejection is worth keeping in full, because "release weekly" is the obvious answer and the reason it fails is not obvious: it optimises the wrong variable. `req:frictionless-update` wants updating to be cheap and routine, and the way to get that is small increments, not frequent checks of a large one.
